body_markdown:
A flash of electric blue ruptures an otherwise dull morning in the hills near Lapalisse, France. The pristine 1965 Renault Caravelle rumbles down the main street, an antique stroller and leather bags strapped tightly on its roof, as if a family were setting off on vacation. A gleaming ’63 Cadillac Sedan de Ville follows on its tail. As the duo halts on the town bridge, shop windows vibrate to the growl of the Caddy’s 6.4-liter V-8.


The town’s authorities give chase: Three policemen, dressed in old-school leather uniforms, catch up on their bikes, blowing their whistles furiously. But their efforts to keep the traffic flowing are in vain. Behind them, the road has transformed into a rainbow of vintage cars.


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


The *Embouteillage Lapalisse* , or Lapalisse Traffic Jam, helps cars, traditions, and the village come alive for a new generation. But it’s not a car *show* , per se. More like organized, 20-mile-long gridlock. Thousands of classic-car enthusiasts descend on this small village to celebrate the golden age of French motoring, when affordable family cars like the Renault 4L, Citroën DS, 2CV, and Peugeot 404 put the French middle class on the road. In the 1950s and 1960s, as these families headed to the Riviera for their summer holidays, the traffic was famously brutal.


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


Held every two years in this sleepy corner of central France, the Traffic Jam shuts down Lapalisse, a village of 3000 souls, for an entire October weekend. More than 1000 classic cars attend, and the schedule includes an auction and a *concours d’élégance* .


Old horns bark as a ’62 Citroën DS carrying a kayak tries to pass a ’67 Mustang convertible. Costumed nuns, priests, and rabbis weave through the rows of traffic on antique Peugeot *cyclomoteurs* (mopeds), as passengers abandon their vehicles and pull foldable chairs out of their trunks. Main Street is thick with the rich aroma of idling carbureted engines.


Antoine Goullin


Fuel was cheap in the ‘50s and ‘60s, but cars were slow, and Lapalisse, which sits on the legendary N7 highway to the French Riviera, became a renowned pit stop. As the country transformed, newly connected by roads and cars capable of traveling them, Lapalisse’s restaurants, hotels, and gas stations boomed.


Over time, things changed. Alternate routes bypassing the town contributed to the town hollowing out by the 2000s. Thierry Dubois, who created the event in 2006, grew nostalgic. “I thought it might be fun to do one final traffic jam, because after that, you know… there won’t be any more,” Dubois says.


Twenty years later, he admits underestimating the durability of the emotion that drives all such reenactments. “Nostalgia… is clearly the past without all the downsides, because I remember the car jams of the ’60s. It was hot and I wanted it to be over,” he says. “Here, it’s more about getting to spend a weekend living truly outside of time.”


Antoine Goullin


So we beat on, Renaults against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past… What began as a perhaps rose-colored tribute to a bygone era has grown into a new tradition, attracting people too young to remember the N7 in its heyday. For an aging village and its cars, the event has brought something absolutely invaluable: a new generation who badly wants to take the wheel.


As the streets fill with visitors, we spot one of these young enthusiasts. Nathan, 17, is speaking with a costumed cop wanting to confirm that he is old enough to drive. “I have my licence,” Nathan laughs. “I’m here thanks to my dad, who gave me this love of old cars,” he says. He is proudly driving a member of the holy trinity of French postwar cars: a *café* colored 2CV, or “ *deux chevaux”* —literally “two horses.” The name refers to its French fiscal horsepower rating, a tax classification rather than its actual engine power.


Antoine Goullin


The adorable vehicle, powered by an air-cooled, flat-twin four-stroke engine, provokes an immediate rush of dopamine in French people. “It’s incredible to be able to drive a part of motoring history. I can see myself owning one of these much more than a modern car. It’s a sound, a feel you just don’t get with new cars,” Nathan gushes.


There’s another reason young people in France are drawn to the Lapalisse jam, and to classic cars in general: price. While young-driver insurance can be quite expensive, “a collector-car policy makes \[insurance\] very affordable for a first car. Of course, it’s even cheaper if you fix up a banged-up one!” Nathan says. Relative accessibility helps keep France’s tradition of youth motoring clubs alive, bringing young enthusiasts together for organised road trips in classic cars.


We march on between the rows of cars, coming across a quirky, matchbox-sized 1939 New Map “Baby” microcar that has given up the ghost at the roadside. “She overheated,” laughs Alexis, the roadster’s owner, who barely fits inside the 1.25-metre-tall car. “It is a traffic jam after all!”


Antoine Goullin


In general, the French take care of their old idols, even the ones from overseas. “It’s a Willys Jeep \[MB\], but not just any Willys Jeep,” Charles, 65, says with an enormous smile. “This one landed in France in July 1944 to help liberate the country. A Nazi chaser, a forward-deployed vehicle that would head out ahead of the tanks… A true icon.” Charles found the Willys in a sorry state at auction five years ago. With a close friend, he rebuilt it piece by piece, tracking down even its original rivets halfway across the world.


Another young gearhead sits beside Charles, his granddaughter, Lisa, 17. She drinks in his words. This is her third Traffic Jam, and this time she is actively scouting for an affordable model of her own. “New cars, especially EVs, are completely unaffordable. No one wants to buy second-hand electric cars because of the constant innovation, yet even the used market is too expensive,” Lisa says. “Besides, I’d much rather fix up a classic. For the climate as well, there’s also a real recycling mindset to it,” she adds.


Antoine Goullin


Antoine Goullin


It’s time for lunch, which showcases the French’s great preparedness when it comes to car picnics. Every vehicle has come equipped—one with its own wine cellar and a *jambon* -cutting board at the back, another with a foldable picnic table that rises out of the trunk. After a generous regional meal, we hop on our second ride of the day, ideal for an easy digestion: a 1974 Citroën DS.


It’s ridiculously elegant and undeniably French, though the long, sculpted bodywork, low roofline, and sweeping curves were designed by an Italian. The groundbreaking self-levelling hydropneumatic suspension lends a magical softness, especially over rough roads. Add its single-spoke steering wheel, and, on later models, swivelling headlights, and it’s easy to see why the Citroën DS seemed like a UFO landing on French roads in 1955.


Antoine Goullin


Vincent, the Citroën’s owner, though more adult than our prior interlocutors, is still too young to have experienced the era the event aims to recreate. He was born in the Nineties, so what exactly is he chasing at the Traffic Jam? “These cars just have personalities. Even when I was a kid, they just had a different status; they were almost a part of the family… When my parents and I sold a car, we cried. Now they’ve become throwaway products,” he adds.


Antoine Goullin


Nostalgia can be a double-edged sword in the automobile world. Clinging to the past can stifle innovation, particularly among French carmakers, which seem to struggle to recapture the ingenuity behind the models they produced well into the late 2000s. Take the electric Renault Twingo and Renault 5: fun modern cars in their own right, but homages nonetheless, their appeal resting partly on the legacy of their predecessors. Lapalisse is a more palatable mix of old and new, the past serving as a starting point to celebrate a town’s history while nourishing its present.


Mayor Stéphanie Chervin, who we meet at the town’s tourism office, away from the bustle and honking, understands that dynamic. “Of course, you have to be crazy to want to reenact a traffic jam,” she says with a cackle. “But it’s really been a way for us to develop our economy.” The event has contributed to a major reversal of the town’s fortunes, which were at their worst when the traffic bypass around town was completed in 2006. “Overnight, all the trucks and through-traffic vanished from the town. It was very disturbing. Business owners, gas station operators in particular, became worried,” Chervin says.


Antoine Goullin


The shift from busy road stop to complete silence was a rough transition for Lapalisse, and many roadstops like it. The village sits in a stretch of France known as the *Line of Emptiness,* an economically poor, aging, and depopulating part of the country. It risked becoming another sad story on that stretch of land.


Now, the name is known to most car enthusiasts in France. With the roughly 40,000 visitors who came to the event over the weekend, the village is most definitely on the map as a touristing spot. The young people are, of course, seen as particularly valuable for the village, and the Traffic Jam has naturally evolved to keep them interested. The event expanded its allowed categories to include “Youngtimer” cars from the ’80s and ’90s that have become trendy with under-40s from the region.


Antoine Goullin


We thought it appropriate to ask Mayor Chervin whether she—a non-car person, by her own admission—had been affected by the exposure to all of this classic car frenzy. “It’s a fantastic adventure; you meet such wonderful, passionate people,” Chervin says.


And what’s her favorite ride? “Myself, I dream of owning a 2CV. I’ve actually been keeping an eye out. My grandfather had a blue one…. He’d head off on holiday, no camping, no tents. He’d take out the seats and set them up right on the beach. He’d sit completely relaxed there, having his lunch. It was fantastic, truly fantastic.”
